newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Petronas says not buying BHP stake in Dai Hung.
newsitem.headline: Petronas says not buying BHP stake in Dai Hung.

text.p: Malaysian state oil company Petroliam Nasional Bhd (Petronas) said on Thursday it has no plans as of now to buy Broken Hill Proprietary Co Ltd's stake in Vietnam's Dai Hung oilfield.

"There are no discussions about buying BHP's stake," Petronas President Hassan Marican said in reply to questions from reporters after announcing the company's financial results for the year ended March 31, 1996.
Asked if Petronas was at all interested in the idea, Hassan said: "We'll cross that bridge when we come to it."

Petronas began producing oil from Dai Hung in 1994. Hassan said the field was thought to have had enormous potential five years ago, around 700 million barrels after the first exploration well was drilled. "We've downgraded it," he said, adding that it was still a commercially viable field.

The Dai Hung field is owned by a consortium comprising BHP with a 43.75-percent stake, Petronas with 20 percent, Vietnam's state-owned PetroVietnam with 15 percent, Total SA and Sumitomo Corp with 10.625 percent each.

Doubts clouded BHP's participation in the consortium when in June the Australian company said the future of the offshore oilfield development was under question, unless talks on the tax regime with PetroVietnam and further drilling could be resolved.

BHP has sought an easier tax regime on the field, which has had estimated reserves cut to 100 million barrels from 800 million barrels. BHP said in June the Dai Hung field is producing about 15,000 barrels per day (bpd) of oil .

PetroVietnam had said in response that it was ready to negotiate further with BHP. It's president Ho Si Thoang said he had not been informed by BHP of any decision and a full evaluation of the reserves had still not been conducted.

Hassan also said Petronas Carigali, the company's exploration arm, had made considerable commercial discoveries during the year at its other Vietnamese concessions. These are the Ruby, Emerald and Topaz fields in Block 01 and 02 offshore Vung Tau, which are 100 percent owned and operated by Petronas.

The Ruby field, which is being developed in two phases, is expected to yield estimated reserves of about 200 million barrels of oil and 0.4 trillion cubic feet of associated gas in the first phase. Oil production is due to begin by 1997 at the rate of 9,500 bpd.
Petronas entered into several overseas exploration and production joint ventures over the past year, Hassan said.
It signed a Farm-in agreement and a Joint Operating agreement for oil and gas exploration in Blocks A and B in the Cotabato and Agusan Davao Basins in the Philippines.
Petronas also signed a deal with the Pakistan government for onshore oil and gas exploration in the Fort Abbas block.
Hassan said an agreement with India would be announced in November, but did not give details. In March, Petronas signed a deal with Indian Oil Corp for downstream activities in India.
Other foreign downstream ventures included a 30-percent stake in a consortium with U.S. Conoco to build a 130,000-bpd refinery at Dung Quat Bay, in central Vietnam.
Petronas is already involved in a joint venture with VietGas to import, store, bottle and market liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) in northern Vietnam with plans to expand to Danang.

Petronas has expanded its chain of petrol stations in Cambodia to 10 and has entered into a joint venture with Unique Gas & Petrochemicals PLC to develop a network of service stations in Thailand under the Petronas brand name.

During the past year, Petronas also entered into joint ventures for LPG projects in the Philippines and China's Jiangsu Province. They involve importing LPG from Malaysia and storing, disributing and marketing the products in the two areas.
